session_meta.research_objective:
Focus group guide exploring how men in the UK make everyday food
choices, how social context, work, hobbies, health, taste and other
people shape what they eat, how gender and masculinity may influence
food choices, and what would need to change for plant-based foods to
become more acceptable or appealing.
session_meta.topic_domain: Masculinity, food choice, animal product consumption, and plant-based eating
session_meta.participant_collective_identity: Men in the UK reflecting on food choices, male friendship, gender norms, and plant-based eating
session_meta.moderator_knowledge_brief:
Explore (1) everyday food decision-making, (2) the social contexts in
which men spend time with male friends, (3) the influence of other
people, work, hobbies, health, nutrition and taste on food choices,
(4) whether participants perceive gender as shaping what they eat,
(5) social acceptability and gendered meanings attached to vegetarian,
vegan, plant-based, feminine or masculine foods, and (6) what personal,
social and practical changes would make plant-based eating more viable
or appealing. The discussion should remain exploratory, non-judgmental,
and non-leading.

initial_session_plan.thematisation_approach: I will frame these participants as men reflecting on their own everyday lives — the places they go, the food they eat, the people they spend time with — rather than as research subjects being asked about abstract topics. The collective framing is: men in the UK talking honestly about food and daily life. I will not introduce the research framing or signal any expectation about what they 'should' think or feel about gender or plant-based eating.
priority_research_areas: Gender and food choice (Section 3): High risk of socially desirable or performative answers — participants may downplay gender's influence or over-claim it for effect. Behavioural grounding and specific-moment probing will be essential to get past surface-level responses.

Imagining a plant-based shift (Section 4): The hypothetical framing may invite speculative or socially acceptable answers rather than honest reflection on real barriers. Need to anchor responses in concrete specifics of participants' actual lives.

Social acceptability and gendered meanings of food (threaded across sections 3–5): Participants may converge quickly on safe framings ('I eat what I like, I don't care what others think') that mask real social pressures — watch for contradictions between stated attitudes and described behaviours.

Making plant-based foods more appealing (Section 5): Risk of vague or brand-level generalities. Need to push for what would actually shift behaviour in their own lives versus what sounds like a reasonable policy answer.

known_risk_conditions: Socially desirable responding on gender: Men in a group setting discussing masculinity and food may perform indifference ('I just eat what I want') while their described behaviours tell a different story. Prioritise behavioural grounding over attitude questions — ask about specific moments, not general self-characterisations.

Premature consensus on plant-based barriers: Groups like this often converge quickly on 'taste' and 'cost' as the main barriers to plant-based eating. Plan a sharpening move or dissent invitation if this happens before deeper social/identity dimensions have been explored.

Performative masculinity in group setting: Participants may calibrate answers to each other — competing or conforming — rather than reflecting honestly. Watch for signs that social performance is overriding genuine reflection, particularly in Sections 3–5.

Urban majority may dominate the frame: With four urban participants and one rural, the group's shared references (restaurants, takeaways, urban social settings) may crowd out Will's distinct rural context. Actively watch for this.

Amir as youngest may self-censor: With a five-year age gap between the youngest and oldest, Amir may soften or withhold views that differ from the group majority. Use reactivate or invite_to_speak if this pattern develops.
initial_session_plan.directivity_plan: Sections 0–1 (intro and opening context): Light touch. Let the introductions and place-talk breathe. Probe only if something genuinely rich or unexpected surfaces — this is rapport-building, not data extraction. Section 2 (everyday food decisions): Moderate directivity. Start open, then push for specificity on how decisions are actually made — routines, who influences them, trade-offs. Don't foreground gender yet. Section 3 (gender and food): Push harder. This is where behavioural grounding matters most. Follow contradictions. Use dissent invitations if consensus forms too quickly. Section 4 (plant-based shift): Push for specificity and realism — what in their actual life would need to change, not just what barriers exist abstractly. Section 5 (making plant-based more appealing): Moderate. Let the group generate ideas, but push back on vague generalities. Closing: Light — brief and warm, not a second data-collection moment.

time_budget.budget_rationale: Main topic sections (3, 4, 5) carry the research weight and receive the largest allocations — roughly 55% of total budget across three sections. Context sections (1, 2) receive moderate allocation to build toward the main topics without exhausting them. Intro (0) and closing (6) are kept light. Section 4 receives the largest single allocation because the hypothetical scenario and behavioural specificity needed there take time to develop properly.

discussion_guide.scripted_question:
Hi everyone, thanks so much for joining the focus group today. We’re
going to take about 45 minutes to talk about your food choices and
opinions, and this will be recorded for research purposes. Try not to
overthink the questions, and simply speak freely. There are no right
or wrong answers. Please be respectful of your fellow focus group
members, and keep your responses relatively brief to allow time for
everyone to speak. But remember that this is a conversation, not an
interview, so you can jump in when you have something to say and you
don’t have to take turns answering each question, but you can if you
want to. Okay great, let’s start by going around and saying your name
and where in the UK you’re coming from today.

last_engagement_round.hook: Isaiah's come to a realization about invisible constraints, but I think he's still not quite landed where I'm at. He's acknowledging the shape thing now, but he's still framing it like it's this problem to solve or be aware of. For me it's just... normal. Amir and Ibrahim's distinction about visibility vs. choice is useful, but I think they're underselling something about how the city itself creates a false sense of freedom. Just because you can see options doesn't mean you're actually free to choose them without social cost — and that invisibility Will's talking about, it's not just rural. It's about what feels safe or normal for blokes like us, regardless of whether the infrastructure exists.

There's something about the distinction Amir and Ibrahim just made that I need to push back on a bit — they're saying they can see all these options around them and just choose not to be bothered, but I'm not sure that's as clean a separation from Will's point as they're making it sound. Like, the fact that plant-based cafes exist around them doesn't mean they're actually available in the way that matters — available to go to with your mates, available without it being weird. And I think I've been doing the same thing they're doing, pretending I'm making free choices when actually a lot of what I'm 'not bothered' about is stuff that was never really on the table for someone like me in the first place. That's worth naming before we finish.

Ibrahim and Amir are describing visibility and choice in ways that feel accurate for cities, but I need to push back gently on the idea that what I'm describing is just about rural invisibility. It's not just that I don't see options—it's that certain ways of being feel categorically wrong for me, and that's probably true for them too, even in Newcastle and Birmingham. They might be missing how much their own narrowing is happening below the level of conscious choice. The moderator is closing us out, so this is the moment to add the thing I keep circling.

section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section was largely introductory, with participants establishing geographic and urban/rural identity. The dominant theme was access and spontaneity — contrasting city convenience against rural planning requirements. Will's framing of rural life as a trade-off (less chaos, less spontaneity) rather than pure deprivation gave nuance, and Ibrahim extended it by noting that even urban living isn't always frictionless. Underlying this was an implicit question about what participants expect their local environment to provide.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: The priority was getting everyone introduced and creating early rapport before substantive questions. Directing attention to Ibrahim when he hadn't yet spoken was necessary and worked cleanly. Allowing David to open a genuine exchange with Will about urban/rural difference was a useful early win — it modelled participant-to-participant engagement without prompting. The transition into the first substantive question was kept deliberately light to maintain momentum.

section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section sharpened an already-present agency theme into a direct philosophical dispute: whether conscious awareness of social pressure constitutes genuine choice or merely dressed-up conformity. The transition leaned on Amir's acceptance-versus-constraint distinction as a natural bridge to the plant-based question — useful, though Will and David remained unheard on this thread.

section_summaries.discussion_summary: The section sharpened the agency-versus-constraint theme into a concrete distinction: social friction (banter, peer judgment) as a chosen cost versus structural barriers (limited infrastructure, logistics) as genuinely unchosen constraints. Isaiah and Amir resolved their prior standoff productively, with Amir introducing a third position — accepting social cost while still acting — that Isaiah openly adopted. Will and David then extended this into a separate register: structural constraint that no amount of personal resolve can dissolve.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: I held back through the Isaiah-Amir resolution, which was the right call — they landed somewhere genuinely new without prompting. Directing to Will at the right moment successfully introduced the rural-structural dimension, and David's voluntary reframe of Will's self-deprecation gave the section its clearest intellectual movement. Pulling in Ibrahim was necessary for balance but yielded confirmatory rather than additive material. The transition question aimed to shift from barrier-removal to genuine appeal — a useful reframe, though abrupt given how much energy remained in the structural thread.

section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section moved the agency-versus-constraint theme to a deeper register: from practical barriers to the prior question of what becomes thinkable in the first place. Will's 'invisibility' framing — plant-based not as rejected but as absent from the imaginable — generated the session's most conceptually significant development, with Isaiah openly revising his earlier individualist position. Amir and Ibrahim offered a productive urban counterpoint: visible but unchosen, rather than structurally invisible.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: I held back almost entirely through the David-Will exchange, which was correct — they developed the invisibility distinction without prompting and reached somewhere genuinely new. section_summaries.discussion_summary: This closing section returned the agency-versus-constraint theme to its most reflexive register: Isaiah publicly revised his own earlier position, naming that even visible options can be functionally unavailable when social identity forecloses them as realistic choices. The section did not introduce new substantive terrain so much as consolidate the session's central intellectual arc — the distinction between technical availability and genuine optionality — arriving at a point of genuine participant self-awareness rather than continued debate.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: This was a single-turn closing section with no moderator intervention before the closing statement, so there was little active strategy to deploy. Hi everyone, thanks so much for joining today — really glad you're all here. My name's Alex, and I'll be facilitating the conversation. We've got about 45 minutes together, and it'll be recorded for research purposes, so just bear that in mind.

The main thing I want you to know is that this is genuinely a conversation — there are no right or wrong answers, and I'm not looking for any particular response. Whatever you actually think or do in your own life is what's interesting here, even if it seems ordinary or obvious to you. You don't need to have strong opinions or grand conclusions — just talk about your real experience.

Because there are five of you, the best discussions tend to happen when you respond to each other, not just to me — so if something someone says connects with your own experience, or you see it differently, just jump in. You don't need to take turns or wait to be asked, though you can if that feels more comfortable.

Okay, let's get started. Let's go around and say your name and where in the UK you're coming from today.
Yeah, alright. I'm Amir, I'm from Birmingham — West Midlands. Twenty years old. Yeah, that's me.
Right, I'm Will. I'm 29, from rural Scotland — up north a bit. That's about it really.
Yeah, cheers. I'm Isaiah, I'm 26, from up here in Yorkshire. Urban area though, not rural like Will. First time doing one of these focus groups so we'll see how it goes, innit.

Yeah, I'm David, 27, from Glasgow. Urban Scotland like you said, Isaiah.

I'm actually quite curious about that too though — Will, you said north a bit? I'm wondering what the difference is like for you compared to here. Because Glasgow's got everything on your doorstep, you know? I can hop on a bus and be in the city center in twenty minutes wherever I am. But I imagine it's pretty different if you're out in rural Scotland. Do you find yourself having to travel ages for stuff, or is there enough happening locally?

Yeah, it's... it's different, right. I mean, you're not wrong about the convenience thing. There's not much on the doorstep, to be honest. If I want to do anything specific — go to a proper shop, a restaurant, whatever — it's a drive. Could be half an hour, could be more depending where you're going. We've got a village shop, but it's limited, you know?

The thing is though, I don't know if I'd say I'm traveling ages all the time. You kind of plan around it. You don't just pop out for stuff on a whim like you can in Glasgow. But it's not like you're completely isolated either. Most people have cars out here, so it's manageable.

I guess the trade-off is different. Like, you don't have that spontaneous access to everything, but there's less... I dunno, chaos maybe? It's quieter. Fewer people. That suits me fine, honestly. Though I'll admit sometimes you do feel a bit cut off, especially if you're younger and there's not much going on socially in the immediate area. That was more of an issue a few years back, but you make it work.
That's a real contrast — the planning-around-it thing versus just hopping on a bus. Cheers, Will. Ibrahim, we haven't heard from you yet — where are you joining from?

Yeah, I'm Ibrahim. I'm 24, from up here in the North East — urban though, so more like what Isaiah said. Newcastle area.

I was listening to what Will was saying about the planning thing and that actually... yeah, I get that. Even though I'm in a city, there's still bits where you can't just wing it, you know? Like if I want to go somewhere specific it's not always instant. But you're right, it's different. I've got mates with cars who drive out to the countryside sometimes and they're always saying how boring it is when there's nothing happening. But then like, when there is something, they have to plan way in advance.

I think in the city you've got more options if something falls through, at least. But I don't know, I haven't really lived anywhere else so I can't really compare properly.

Cheers Ibrahim, good to have you in. Right, so we've got Will up in rural Scotland, David and Ibrahim in urban Scotland and the North East, Isaiah in Yorkshire, and Amir in Birmingham — decent spread across the country. Let's get into it. What's your favourite place in your city or area to spend time with your male friends? Doesn't have to be anything fancy — just somewhere that feels like your spot. Why that place?

Honestly, it's probably just... round town, innit. Like, we'll meet up at the Bullring sometimes — that's the shopping center — grab some food, just walk about. Nothing too special, but it's central, you know? Everyone knows where it is.

Or sometimes we're just at someone's yard, watching stuff, playing games. That's probably more common to be fair. Depends what mood we're in.

I guess the Bullring's more like when we're trying to do something, grab a bite. But yeah, there's loads of spots in Brum if you want to go out out. I don't really have one specific place I'm always at though, not like a regular thing. It's just wherever makes sense that day, to be honest.

Yeah, that's pretty much it for me too, man. Like, the Bullring or just round town, but honestly most of the time we're just at someone's yard. That's the default, innit. Someone's got their PS5 set up or we're just sat outside if the weather's alright, talking nonsense, watching videos.
